title: Presenting your own point of view

match.reason: The bank point teaches analysing a writer's techniques in written paragraphs, while the new point asks students to plan and present their own spoken argument for an audience, which is a different skill.

draft.title: Presenting your own point of view
card: Start by planning. Decide your main point, who your audience is, and what you want them to think or do.
Choose arguments that suit the audience. Pick reasons and examples that they care about and can follow.
Choose techniques to match. A story can make a point real for classmates, and a statistic can help with an audience who want proof.
When you present, use your voice on purpose. Pace, pauses and emphasis help the audience hear your main points.
draft.remember: Plan for your audience, then pick arguments and techniques that suit them.

a.q: Mia will speak to her class about why they should recycle more. What should she do first?
opts: Decide her main point and think about her audience
Choose a technique before knowing her point
Write the ending and skip the planning
Read out facts that she finds boring
a.why: Planning starts with a clear main point and a sense of the audience. Choosing a technique first is tempting, but it cannot fit the audience until she knows her point and who is listening.
a.clue: What does a speaker need to know before choosing anything else?

b.q: Jack must persuade the school council, who want proof, to fund a new bike shed. Which choice suits this audience best?
opts: Use figures on how many students ride to school
Tell a long joke about his own bike
Appeal only to how nice a shed would look
Speak quickly so he finishes sooner
b.why: The council wants proof, so figures on student numbers give them reasons they can weigh. A story or joke may entertain, but it does not meet what this audience wants.
b.clue: What does this audience want to see?

a.best: Decide her main point and think about her audience

b.best: Use figures on how many students ride to school

problems.detail: The distractors are implausible for Year 11 ('Write the ending and skip the planning', 'Read out facts that she finds boring'), so students can pick the answer without understanding audience-based planning.

The distractors ('Speak quickly so he finishes sooner', 'Tell a long joke about his own bike') are obviously poor choices. The question tests common sense rather than matching technique to audience, which is too easy for Year 11.

Choose arguments that suit the audience. Pick reasons and examples that they care about and can follow, not just the ones you like best.
Choose techniques to match. A story can make a point real for classmates, and a statistic can help with an audience who want proof.
When you present, use your voice on purpose. Pace, pauses and emphasis help the audience hear your main points.
proposal.remember: Plan for your audience, then pick arguments and techniques that suit them.

a.q: Mia has chosen her main point for a speech to Year 7 students. What should guide her choice of arguments?
opts: What her Year 7 listeners care about and can follow
Which reasons she finds the most convincing herself
Which reasons sound the most complex and impressive
Which reasons her own teacher used in class
a.why: Arguments should be chosen for the audience, so Mia needs reasons Year 7 students care about and can follow. Picking the reasons she finds most convincing is tempting, but her listeners may not share her concerns.
a.clue: Who does the speech need to persuade?

b.q: Jack wants the school council to fund a bike shed. Members say they back only projects with clear evidence. What should he use?
opts: Survey results on how many students ride to school
A personal story about his bike being stolen at school
A lively description of how much students love cycling
His own strong opinion, repeated with firm emphasis
b.why: This audience wants proof, so survey figures give them evidence they can weigh. A personal story is tempting because it makes the problem feel real, but it is one case, not the evidence this council asks for.
b.clue: What kind of support does the card link to an audience who want proof?

a.best: What her Year 7 listeners care about and can follow
